Klee's unsettling effect, for me, has to do with this naive style applied to adult concerns, all with a bit of a sinister edge.

I think his more mechanical drawings are a bit easier to get.

I have a print of his Alter Dampfer (https://api.nga.gov/iiif/c33297dc-45d8-441c-b09e-36944e33f61c/full/!800,800/0/default.jpg) on my wall. You might imagine a child gazing at a steamboat, or any modern contraption and rendering something like this, where the mechanical components are recognizable but their connections and functions are mysterious. You could say this is a metaphor for man in modernity.

Another favorite is Twittering Machine (https://www.moma.org/collection/works/37347). Birds are mechanized, hooked to a crank, made to sing their song on command. Do they look happy? Tortured? It's hard to say. And on top of it all, there's the childish playfulness of the style -- the Twittering Machine is perhaps fun to use!

And I'd suggest that "contextually *driven*" is stronger language than we should be using here. Context always exists -- none of our experience happens in a cultural or linguistic vacuum -- but context will often nuance rather than drive our experience. In some cases our awareness of context is so minimal that even nuance might be too strong a word.

If all you know about Chesterton is that he's writing in English and has an Anglo name, those are probably not major factors in your aesthetic reaction to his work. Even more so when you're responding to an image or sculpture or building without knowing its provenance.

It's cool to learn about the wider context of things. And I'm all for humanism of the "humani nil a me alienum puto" stripe --for trying to understand why other people have poured passion and resources into creating something that initially strikes you as ugly or unimpressive.

But at the end of the day, I don't believe in the superiority of art that you can really *only* appreciate with a laboriously-achieved awareness of its context -- Joyce's Ulysses or Eliot's Waste Land, for example, or architecture whose intentional ugliness is best defended by an excursus into history. Not saying it's inherently inferior, mind you. Just that the "holistic" experience of art-in-dialogue-with-other-art is neither inevitable nor superior to an aesthetic experience unmediated by awareness of that context.

You want to write an epic about the present, but epics have usually been about the legendary past, not the present.

The Trojan War was 400 years old to Homer, and even more ancient to later Greeks and Romans, who continued to write epics and other works using that setting, for example the Aeneid or the Oresteia.

Throughout the late Middle Ages and Renaissance, countless epics were written about the Matter of France and the Matter of Britain, respectively the times of Charlemagne and Arthur, ancient at that point.

Fantasy itself stems from that tradition. There is a continuous production of Arthurian material throughout the last thousand years or thereabouts, and when someone today writes an Arthurian story, everyone calls it "fantasy".

There is even a connection through Tolkien, who (I believe) thought of himself as writing in the epic tradition. Indeed, his Middle Earth is explicitly the past of our Earth, his elves and dwarves the elves and dwarves of our world.

There are two ways to write an epic today and be taken seriously.

The first one is to make it "fantasy". I've always wanted to write one in an Arthurian setting, either wholly in verse, or in a mixture of prose and verse. It would be simultaneously an imitation of past works (by Renaissance authors writing about mythical dark ages, e.g. Orlando Furioso), and a contemporary fantasy. If Tolkien can have bits of verse in his novels so can any fantasy author, stretch that principle and you get a whole fantasy epic in verse. Fantasy fans would love it. The only reason I'm never gonna do it is that AI is already ending all human art, so there is no point.

The other way to be taken seriously is to rely on genres of poetry that thrive today, such as rap albums or musical drama. If you write an epic as a musical, you can even make it about present day themes.

I want to find out what sort of picture we shall get by reversing the process. Let us make our distinction between readers or types of reading the basis, and our distinction between books the corollary. Let us try to discover how far it might be plausible to define a good book as a book which is read in one way, and a bad book as a book which is read in another.

I think this worth trying because the normal procedure seems to me to involve almost continually a false implication. If we say that A likes (or has a taste for) the women’s magazines and B likes (or has a taste for) Dante, this sounds as if likes and taste have the same meaning when applied to both; as if there were a single activity, though the objects to which it is directed are different. But observation convinces me that this, at least usually, is untrue.

...Some critics write of those who constitute the literary ‘many’ as if they belonged to the many in every respect, and indeed to the rabble. They accuse them of illiteracy, barbarism, ‘crass’, ‘crude’ and ‘stock’ responses which (it is suggested) must make them clumsy and insensitive in all the relations of life and render them a permanent danger to civilisation. It sometimes sounds as if the reading of ‘popular’ fiction involved moral turpitude. I do not find this borne out by experience. I have a notion that these ‘many’ include certain people who are equal or superior to some of the few in psychological health, in moral virtue, practical prudence, good manners, and general adaptability. And we all know very well that we, the literary, include no small percentage of the ignorant, the caddish, the stunted, the warped, and the truculent. With the hasty and wholesale apartheid of those who ignore this we must have nothing to do.

If it had no other defect it would still be too diagrammatic. The two sorts of readers are not cut off by immovable barriers. Individuals who once belonged to the many are converted and join the few. Others desert from the few to the many, as we often sadly discover on meeting an old schoolfellow. Those who are on the ‘popular’ level as regards one art may be deeply appreciative of another; musicians sometimes have deplorable preferences in poetry. And many whose responses to all the arts are trivial may yet be people of great intelligence, learning and subtlety.

...Still less is the status seeker. As there are, or were, families and circles in which it was almost a social necessity to display an interest in hunting, or county cricket, or the Army List, so there are others where it requires great independence not to talk about, and therefore occasionally to read, the approved literature, especially the new and astonishing works, and those which have been banned or have become in some other way subjects of controversy. Readers of this sort, this ‘small vulgar’, act in one respect exactly like those of the ‘great vulgar’. They are entirely dominated by fashion. They drop the Georgians and begin to admire Mr Eliot, acknowledge the ‘dislodgement’ of Milton, and discover Hopkins, at exactly the right moment. They will not like your book if the dedication begins with To instead of For. Yet, while this goes on downstairs, the only real literary experience in such a family may be occurring in a back bedroom where a small boy is reading Treasure Island under the bed-clothes by the light of an electric torch.

...Real appreciation demands the opposite process. We must not let loose our own subjectivity upon the pictures and make them its vehicles. We must begin by laying aside as completely as we can all our own preconceptions, interests, and associations. We must make room for Botticelli’s Mars and Venus, or Cimabue’s Crucifixion, by emptying out our own. After the negative effort, the positive. We must use our eyes. We must look, and go on looking till we have certainly seen exactly what is there. We sit down before the picture in order to have something done to us, not that we may do things with it. The first demand any work of any art makes upon us is surrender. Look. Listen. Receive. Get yourself out of the way. (There is no good asking first whether the work before you deserves such a surrender, for until you have surrendered you cannot possibly find out.)

It is not only our own ‘ideas’ about, say, Mars and Venus which must be set aside. That will make room only for Botticelli’s ‘ideas’, in the same sense of the word. We shall thus receive only those elements in his invention which he shares with the poet. And since he is after all a painter and not a poet, this is inadequate. What we must receive is his specifically pictorial invention: that which makes out of many masses, colours, and lines the complex harmony of the whole canvas.

The distinction can hardly be better expressed than by saying that the many use art and the few receive it. The many behave in this like a man who talks when he should listen or gives when he should take. I do not mean by this that the right spectator is passive. His also is an imaginative activity; but an obedient one. He seems passive at first because he is making sure of his orders. If, when they have been fully grasped, he decides that they are not worth obeying—in other words, that this is a bad picture—he turns away altogether.

From the example of the man who uses Tintoretto as pornography it is apparent that a good work of art may be used in the wrong way. But it will seldom yield to this treatment so easily as a bad one. Such a man will gladly turn from Tintoretto to Kirchner or photographs if no moral or cultural hypocrisy prevents him. They contain fewer irrelevancies; more ham and less frill.

But the reverse is, I believe, impossible. A bad picture cannot be enjoyed with that full and disciplined ‘reception’ which the few give to a good one. This was borne in upon me lately when I was waiting at a bus stop near a hoarding and found myself, for a minute or so, really looking at a poster —a picture of a man and a girl drinking beer in a public house. It would not endure the treatment. Whatever merits it had seemed to have at the first glance diminished with every second of attention. The smiles became waxwork grins. The colour was, or seemed to me, tolerably realistic, but it was in no way delightful. There was nothing in the composition to satisfy the eye. The whole poster, besides being ‘of’ something, was not also a pleasing object. And this, I think, is what must happen to any bad picture if it is really examined."

They're the local optimum, if you will. If I write a Dickensian work, I have to either plagiarize, or I have to make changes that are almost guaranteed to make things worse, because I'm only imitating a style that I'll never truly master, in a dialect I've never even heard a real living person speak. So it follows that I should probably just move away from these clusters and focus on making Bobbersonian works. Will these be better than Homer and Dickens? I think the real question is exactly how far should the Bobbersonian cluster be from the Dickensian cluster? I don't think the distance should be zero, but I do think that modern literary sensibility demands an unreasonably far distance.

Ok so let me try and have a crack at explaining why the analogy with medicine doesn't really make sense to me. The experience of both dining at a restaurant and engaging with art depend on what Ernst Gombrich would call the 'beholder's share': there is a collaborative back-and-forth going on between the viewer/diner and the artwork/meal, in which a specific experience is created in the moment based on their own personal history, emotions, preferences, cultural narratives, etc.

The beholder's share is basically the art history version of Popper's argument that all observations are theory-laden (Gombrich and Popper were great friends). The point being that there is no such thing as a neutral observer: you must always start out with some problem you are trying to solve, even if you're not consciously aware of it.

So we can dissolve a lot of confusion by reminding ourselves that the 'problem situation' that each person finds themselves in will vary wildly. This is is easy to see with something like books or TV shows: my 2yo is working on very different problems than I am! But it is equally true of dining: it sounds like you are interested in solving the highly-constrained problem of "which food tastes best when consumed blindfolded in my own home, with zero other context or sensory data". Most other people's problem-situation will have terms for probably dozens or hundreds of other considerations. The food critic's review is therefore much more useful for solving other people's problems than it is for yours.

Circling back to medicine: the disanalogy is that everyone evaluating a certain drug is in almost the exact same problem situation: they want to cure their cancer (or whatever) with a minimum of side effects. So it makes total sense to be completely fixated on efficacy vs side effects, and give essentially no consideration to anything else.

Pirsig's "Metaphysics of Quality" provides a metaphor, and maybe even a vocabulary, relevant to this. Pirsig said that everything is made of Quality. Quality is divided into Dynamic Quality - generative, new, exploratory - and four kinds of static quality: physical, biological, social, intellectual.

I'd argue that art, as distinct from craft, has to contain Dynamic Quality. But only an interpreter with a context can tell the difference between Dynamic Quality (which, I think, must be connected to static quality) and random noise - or, indeed, between Dynamic Quality and static quality that they've never personally seen.

Also, there are multiple kinds of static quality, and there are multiple kinds of art, from Michelangelo's David to "Piss Christ" to "White on White" to Madonna or Warhol's work.

I think this translates into "Art must contain genuine novelty, and must build on something so the viewer can connect to it" - which is extremely broad, maybe overly broad, but it feels useful.

With regard to the question of derivative work ("Okay, but do you like art?"), I think we should draw a distinction between the impact of a work on the individual, and the amount of credit or social respect that the artist deserves.

As far as an individual viewer's response is concerned, it makes sense that the strongest response to impressionism may be evoked by the first good impressionist works that one encounters. As long as the artist has done a competent job executing the conventions of the genre (not trivial), it is entirely reasonable that the result should have the same emotional effect on a naïve viewer as the original works of Monet would. In both cases, the experience is that of discovering impressionism for the first time.

On the other hand, even if the derivative artist's work is just as good as Monet's, it makes sense that Monet gets more credit. Monet (and contemporaries) had to invent the style of impressionism and figure out how to execute it without existing examples to copy or refer to. Even if there are many people who each have their own favourite impressionist works, or even if your real favourite artist is the AI image generator that can spit out impressionist versions of whatever scene you request, it makes sense that you and all other impressionist fans can agree to revere Monet as a founder of the movement you enjoy and as the inspiration without whom your favourite works might not exist in the same form.

This is a matter of coordination. It wouldn't be socially possible to coordinate the same level of respect and reverence for other derivative impressionists because there are too many of them and which one made the most impact on someone probably depends idiosyncratically on the order one encountered them.

Then again, among devoted fans of a genre or style, it makes sense that originality may be less important than sheer quality. All impressionism fans already know Monet and his work is no longer novel or exciting to them. So if some new artist comes along doing equally good work, it is natural that the new artist may be celebrated within that niche community. And I think this actually does happen. I don't know too much about the Impressionism appreciation community, but for example with music fans or video game fans, there can be lots of excitement about new releases within a specific genre, even though it's unlikely that the new release will get the same widespread acclaim as the defining works of the genre. And if the new releases are unique or innovative in some way, then they may themselves inspire imitators and become new definitive benchmarks for their own niche.

Think of Art as a flow of Shannonian information, bits, that a receptor with limited processing power has to parse. Abstract concepts such as "Impressionism" or "pacing" work as filters which help you group bits of information into "chunks" which are easier to parse. The endgame is not to reduce all information to just one easy-to-parse concept, because that just gets boring. Oh, it's just Impressionism, whatever. But it's also not to trascend the need for abstract concepts. Because if the information is too much for you then you may get overloaded or anxious. No good. You want to get to that sweetspot, that Mihály-Csíkszentmihályi-flow-state of aesthethic contemplation where it just clicks. Where it's still challenging, but you feel like you have the tools to make sense of it.

Notably, different filters break down information in different ways. Some abstract paintings require specific filters to be appreciated. Breaking them down with the wrong filter just produces a boring picture. Oh, my five year old could've paint that. Whatever. Also, the space you phisically occupy and your psycho-sensory state and profile also act like filters. If you're high or are autistic you just see a different work of art. The music of a string quartet gets lost in an open field. You need a quiet, enclosed space to really appreciate it. Pop music with simple melodies and simple lyrics needs a show of lights and dancing and costumes and set pieces (more information) to not bore it's audience.

Great art which persists over the centuries sort of automatically adjusts to where you are. If you know nothing, then just the immediate big picture is pleasant and its complexities are safely hidden away. But as you learn more, it grows with you. You, again, literally see a different work of art that someone who knows nothing. You don't grow past Shakespeare, as you would with, say, Harry Potter. Harry Potter gets destroyed by all sorts of conceptual filters. Shakespeare gives you interesting returns basically no matter which filters you apply to it. Even filters which didn't exist when the work was created. Feminism, psychoanalysis, bear biology.

I agree with Scott that art that exists to question "what is art" isn't that interesting. However, I feel that he overestimates the amount of modern art that does this.

Instead, I would posit that 3) Pattern Language and 7) Political And Ideological Point-Making are, and have been for a very long time, the primary driving forces behind art, both modern and pre-modern.

In the 18th and 19th century, the language of art was primarily driven (in Europe) by political institutions. A notable example is the concerted political/critical push in the French academies to change from the visual language of Rococo, which was deemed frivolous and bad for society, to the neoclassical style, which was believed to instill civic virtue. While sensual pleasure and technique was to be found in both styles, the primary change was in the *language* of art. No longer was art communicating about shepherds flirting with women in frilly dresses, now the dialogue is shifted to highlight scenes of civic duty and sacrifice. To reflect this change in politics and ideology, the visual language changed as well -- gone are the soft focus and deep backgrounds, replaced by hard lines and geometric settings. (See David's Oath of the Horatii: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Le_Serment_des_Horaces_-_Jacques-Louis_David_-_Mus%C3%A9e_du_Louvre_Peintures_INV_3692_%3B_MR_1432.jpg/3840px-Le_Serment_des_Horaces_-_Jacques-Louis_David_-_Mus%C3%A9e_du_Louvre_Peintures_INV_3692_%3B_MR_1432.jpg vs Fragonard's The Swing: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/83/The_Swing_%28P430%29.jpg)

If you look at art critics from the period, most of their main criticisms were about the subject matter and how it was depicted (3 and 7) -- due to the academy systems, the top artists all had pristine technique. There was a shared language of art, mostly based on Biblical and mythological scenes. For each artist, political and personal interests are mostly expressed through this shared language of myth. (At art museums, I recommend spending the most time on religious paintings when looking at art from this period -- notice which characters are highlighted or de-emphasized, how they interact, how they're emotionally reacting to what's happening in the scene and how it might compare to the classic readings of Bible stories)

In the modern period, the arts became more and more de-institutionalized and culturally the focus was shifted more towards the individual. Public interest in myth and religion waned. The modern artist doesn't use a shared language -- they develop a personal language and system. This language may be intertextual (4), but renowned artists are usually primarily concerned with developing their own coherent language.

Because modern artists try to build a personal language, if you take any of their pieces and A/B test them like Scott suggests, they're likely to fall flat. This is expected, because you haven't learned how to read the work yet. If you look across the artist's ouvre, things will usually make a lot more sense, even if you don't like it.

For example, take Cy Twombley's Leda and the Swan: https://www.moma.org/collection/works/80083

It looks like nothing. It looks like shit. But, it makes a lot more sense if you see his other works, and realize that one of his primary concerns is with the relationship between visual arts, writing, myth, and the process of symbolization. We see the caligraphy-like looping markings, and the splashes of color evoke a sense of movement and violence. In the corner, there's a window, which is a motif across his work. Out of the cloud of scribbles, you see heart shapes.

Do I *like* it? No, I actually don't, I'm not a fan of his. But I understand and appreciate what he's doing here with his personal language, and my girlfriend, who has spent much more time with his works, loves him. My point here is that Cy Twombley is *not* making art about art. He's making art about violence, gendered violence, about storytelling and myth -- just with an idiosyncratic personal language.

You can say that this idea of "personal artistic language" sucks and we should stop doing it. That would be fine. But I don't think that a conformity-driven spiral of criticism is what you don't like about modern art, and I don't think that there's been any fundamental break (other than some exceptions like Dada) in how artists and critics make and value art.

(Anecdotally, I've heard multiple people say that they didn't like particular artists or modern art in general until seeing a particularly well curated exhibit which "teaches" you how to "read" an artist)

For me, this is the real pleasure of modern art: looking across an artist's work, deciphering their project, and seeing where it ends up.

What I, and I think many people, often desire from art is some form of transcendental experience, where you encounter art that seems to partially part the veil, and you emerge from that experience transformed in some small (or large) way, after seeing capital-B Beauty. What I also value is trying to see art through an empathetic lens. Angelus Novus is a great example of that. Without having read that one person's description I probably wouldn't have put much thought into that work, and I'm not going to go out and buy a print or anything, but seeing it after reading the description connects me to that critic. Criticism, at its best, is a sort of shared sight. The critic "sees" something in the art that they try to communicate, and by viewing art in light of that communication, we can better see what they're seeing. Even if we ultimately believe that what they see isn't entirely justified by the art itself, we've still engaged in an act of empathy. In addition to stretching that empathetic "muscle" we also gain a greater vocabulary for how other people might see art and the world.

Maybe doing this we are occasionally duped by a dishonest and insincere critic or artist, but I think that's a fine price to pay for entering into the collective conversation of art/beauty/aesthetics.

Even if we aren't examining art in light of what someone else has said about it, we can practice seeing art in this way. I try to make it a habit, now, whenever I go to an art museum, to pick a couple of pieces and really look at them. Stand in front of them for 10, 15 minutes, and try to experience that piece in a number of different ways. For a painting I might spend some time thinking about the technical aspects--what do I see in terms of the brush stroke, or the colors used, or the composition? Then go to wherever my mind takes me to try to get into the artist's headspace. Why would someone pick this subject to paint? Look at faces. What do the expressions on the faces tell us about those people? What background details can I see? What do I know about this artist and their place in the history of art? What political, religious, or social topics might have been on their mind at the time? And so on and so forth

I've found that nearly every time I've done this I've not felt it to be a waste of time. Even if most of the answers to the questions I ask myself are, "I have no clue" or "this is confusing", the very act of genuinely spending time with the art is meaningful. For maybe only a brief moment I've tried to step outside myself and see something as someone else might have seen it.

You hit on a pet peeve of mine. I first encountered the idea that art should be evaluated as divorced from context back in a music theory elective I took in college, and it’s sat uneasy with me ever since.

I think it’s because I believe personal transformation is, in fact, inextricably tied to the context in which you encounter the art, (your understanding of) the history that preceded it, and (yes) how novel it is, at least to you.

Let me give an analogy to this blog. At the risk of offending our host, the book review contests gave some of the best content ever published here. A lot of them have stuck with me and have since formed fundamental building blocks of my thought process.

For me, the ones that did this most successfully were the ones that took a scholar’s life work and gave a distilled, accessible introduction to them. After reading Lars Doucet’s review of Progress and Poverty, I can no longer look at the vacant storefronts of San Francisco without thinking “Land value tax would fix this!”. After reading Brandon Hendrickson’s The Educated Mind review I can exactly pinpoint (at least part of) what separated my mediocre teachers from my excellent ones: the best ones looped in Mythic and Romantic elements (including historical stories) to make their lessons much more memorable, like my civil engineering professor telling us about Robert Hooke’s secret anagram “ceiiinosssttuv” as a way to make Hooke’s law memorable.

I think great art often does this as well. It leaves you with a fundamental building block that directly affects your thinking from then on, like the base nutrients in a meal going on to permanently be part of your body. The sensory delights, then, are the seasonings, the spices, the sugar on top of that, which makes the whole dish palatable, and harmonizes with and complements the fundamental flavour of the meal.

If a dish is mostly spices and sugar, it’s just empty calories. It’ll be enjoyable in the moment but is unlikely to stick with you.

A couple of examples:

Fans of this blog might know the online author Wildbow, famous for his online serial “Worm”. But I’ve been reading through a more recent serial of his, “Pale”, a magical fantasy set in contemporary times which I think is actually his best work.

One thing it explores is the concept of the “Faerie-Goblin dichotomy”. In his world, the Faerie are beings of artifice, of glamour, of presentation and poise and status. If Instagram was a fantasy race it would be the Faerie. The goblins, on the other hand, are the dregs of humanity: shit, piss, drunkenness, crass violence, and the grossest parts of sex. Naturally, they hate each other.

Through the Faerie, it explores how living for artifice eventually leads to a sort of self-Flanderization, where one aspect of your public image ends up taking over how you’re seen and ultimately how you see yourself. Through the Goblins, it explores how their grossness can be its own sort of falseness and artifice and status game, meaning the two ends of the spectrum aren’t that distant. One of the human characters is trained by both a Fae and a Goblin, and ends up combining both techniques.

And it wraps all this (and more) in a murder-mystery-slash-coming-of-age story with characters that are stronger and more memorable than in Worm. (And that’s saying something.) That’s the spice.

One of my favourite books is Michael Ende’s “The Neverending Story”. Its core, or at least the part that sticks with me, is that it’s often hard to know what you truly want out of life. It can sometimes take a lifetime of exploration to really figure it out, and some people never even get there in time to achieve it.

It wraps that in a beautifully complementary fantasy story with metafictional elements that hook you into the fundamental mysteries behind its world and makes it clear that a lot of this is, in fact, about you, the reader.

(If you only ever saw the movie, you never caught this part. The first movie is only half the book. Read it, and see if you can find a paper edition that preserves the original red-and-green text colouration, which is a core part of the experience.)

In music, your typical “good sounds” are traditional harmony, ratios of frequencies that sound pleasing to the ear. Its opposite is chromaticism, notes so close to each other that their ratios are out of whack: not a nice 1:2 or 1:3 ratio of frequencies but something like 16:15. There’s a string piece by Krzysztof Penderecki that is absolutely awful to listen to, because it sits on those chromatic chords for minutes on end, ear-piercing screeches making you sick to your stomach until you beg to make it stop.

Then you learn that the title of the piece is “Threnody to the Victims of Hiroshima” and you realize all of that was intentional. The horror you’re feeling is a fraction of the horror those victims felt.

This one, admittedly, has fairly little seasoning. But put it in the right context, prepare yourself for what you’re about to listen to, and it can be transformative nonetheless.

The context can even serve to help bring unusual artistic ideas to a broader audience. The internet has recently gotten kind of obsessed with Angine du Poitrine, a band making microtonal rock music: https://youtu.be/0Ssi-9wS1so

Microtonality is the final boss of chromaticism. Forget the 16:15 semitone, you’re now playing even more dissonant 35:36 quarter-tones which sound even harsher to the ear. How the hell do you make that pleasant enough to listen to that it goes viral?

First, you present yourself as literal aliens bringing strange new music to humanity. I don’t think it’s a coincidence that these folks went viral through video rather than audio. They have polka dot skin paint and masks, bare feet to manipulate their instruments, and a triangle emblem that may or may not be a religious symbol. This gets people into a mood where they say “I don’t understand this yet, but I’m going to keep watching to figure it out, because it’s fascinating.”

Then, you give just enough familiarity for listeners latch onto. In their case, it’s traditional rock vibes that usually come in strong a few minutes into each song. If you’re listening to that link above, give it like 4-5 minutes before writing it off completely. For me, that’s when the fascination turned into enjoyment.

So what’s its core nutrient? In my view, it’s that microtonality and chromaticism can actually sound fun and catchy, even if strange. One of the comments on that YouTube video summed it up best: “The elites don’t want you to know this, but you can just make up your own notes.”

But if that were common in the majority of the music industry, it would not be so fascinating, and that lesson would not be interesting or memorable. We’d have already internalized it. I suspect some Indian or middle-eastern listeners probably already have, and are less likely to be fascinated by Angine du Poitrine.

Returning to my university experience, that music theory class gave us a bunch of tools to analyze music, and had us write a paper using those tools to analyze a song we picked from a list. Context was one of them, but was called out as controversial, for reasons similar to those expressed here.

For that paper, I initially picked some boring orchestral song where I could felt like I could use all the tools. But I couldn’t make it come together. I could talk about the timbre and melody and so on, but it felt like what I had to say about those didn’t cohere into an interesting whole.

So I ultimately dropped it the night before the paper was due and feverishly wrote about the song that actually spoke to my heart, Franz Schubert’s “Gretchen am Spinnrade”, a song for vocals and piano based on a scene in Goethe’s “Faust”: https://youtu.be/kxhpNRZZ7vs

I couldn’t use all the tools as easily, but I brought in the context and it served as the core of the essay: that this is a love song where the love is a BAD thing, which both the lyrics and the musical choices emphasize, all backed by the cyclical sounds of Gretchen’s spinning wheel in the background.

And that’s the core of the song: that love is not always beautiful and healing, but can be dangerous and destructive. I’ve since seen friends fall into that trap and I wish I could have spared them from that fate.

I’m not a poetry buff nor am I familiar with the works of Chesterton. But my suspicion is that part of why you like his poems is that he puts something valuable to you into their core. Maybe a kernel of his principled Christian moral philosophy? And I think more Chesterton poems would add more texture to that, more dimensions, maybe more lessons.

And hopefully, because it’s from the same author at a different point in his development of thought, those lessons don’t really repeat themselves more than they have to. I’m not sure a forgery or someone aping Chesterton’s style would do this.

Artists evolve, they refine their messages, they change their minds and advance their skills. Even Michelangelo had this: the early to mid Sistine chapel paintings had much more optimistic and brighter messages than the later ones, because the later ones were painted when the Protestant reformation was threatening the power of the Catholic church. Hence why “The Last Judgement” depicts a strong, muscular Christ passing final judgement on a world full of sinners.

I’m not sure I’m going to listen to much more Angine du Poitrine, in contrast. A few songs of theirs are enough to get the core message across. (Though who knows, maybe they’ll surprise me.)

Which is also why I agree with you on modern art. I agree that the core message of “Haha, can you believe I can call this transgressive and ugly thing art?” was already played out by the time of the Dadaists, and has no place in something as permanent as architecture. I think it’s time for the pendulum to swing back, even in ways that might seem a bit cringe.

(Even the Renaissance was named such because they felt like they were re-birthing the artistic and scientific spirit of the ancient Romans and Greeks. Maybe it’s time for another one?)

The tricky thing, though, is that this core of value is always relative to the viewer. A kid’s show that says “The true treasure is the friends we made along the way” is horribly cliché and boring, unless you’re a five-year-old that has never seen that message expressed before. That five year old does in fact need to learn that connections to people can sometimes be far more meaningful than material wealth. This is another reason why context, why knowing the target audience, matters.

I cannot defend Angelus Novus, I think it’s weird and kind of ugly. But I suspect that Benjamin is being honest about his praise of it. His Angelus Novus is not the same one we see, because he’s seeing it tinted by his life experience, frameworks, and biases. He’s projecting his own concerns about progress onto the painting, the same way I projected my concerns about life onto “The Neverending Story”. It could just as easily have been a blank canvas, if he were the kind of person to project those concerns onto literal nothingness.

As an artist, you have to pick your audience and meet them where they’re at. What is the core of your art going to target, and who’s going to pay you for making it? The people that have never seen that message before, the people who have seen some of it and want more, or the people who’ve seen a lot of it and think it’s played out, and are hungry for variety?

If you want to draw an analogy to science here, medicine is the wrong analogy. You want to look at social science, especially social science of perception, like the infamous “Dress”.

https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/D2GrrrrfipHWPJSHh/book-review-how-minds-change#:~:text=The%20neuroscientists%20tie,the%20first%20place

No one can agree on whether The Dress in that picture is white/gold vs. blue/black because what you see is dependent on whether you’re a morning or evening person, whether you’re used to seeing items illuminated by yellow indoor lighting or blue noonday sunlight. The Dress has a factual answer: it’s black and blue. Art does not.

Art doesn’t exist on the canvas. It exists in the mind of the person viewing it.

Art is the perception of art.

I don’t think it’s possible to scientifically segment out good art as separate from the context the viewer brings to it. The best you can maybe do is to say which contexts and interpretations are most common in your society and tailor your art towards that. (Architecture in particular could probably benefit from this.)

But if you do that, expect a lot of people on the fringes, especially people who consume a lot of art, to complain that art is boring now and nothing is new. Which frankly doesn’t look too different from what we have today.

I am an art snob that likes Resnais movies and modern art. I actually grew up as a Letterboxd kid.

If I were to probe my subconscious enough, I would probably define a 'good' work of art as a work of art that accurately represents people and psychological dynamics and a 'bad' work of art as a work of art that does not do this. Meaning, even if the world is fake and fantastical: are the psychological profiles of the characters congruous? Could they be people that existed in the real world? Do the decisions they make over the course of the work stay 'in character'? In a movie, do their living spaces fit what they 'are like'? In a novel, do the emotional tendencies of how they think match how they behave around others? Do the characters have the depth and emotion that every person in the real world has in some capacity?

In this frame, the great artists just do accurate representation with hard-to-understand or alien psychologies. Stanley Kubrick accurately represents a sociopath in A Clockwork Orange. Alfred Hitchcock renders a perverted romantic obsessive with high fidelity in Vertigo. Dostoevsky consistently writes depressive, brooding, and narcissistic characters in a way that is vivid enough to where it strikes home for anyone who has had phases like that in their life. This naturally skews negative, as alien psychologies more often lead to suffering than pleasure, but in theory if someone wrote some sweeping 800-page postmodern novel about some rigid and polyamorous Effective Altruist this would also qualify.

Musicians and painters just do this on a smaller scale. Instead of rendering people in fictional worlds, artists and painters are just tasked with invoking feeling. The best people in the world at doing this try to use their skill to invoke hard-to-access or strange feelings. Van Gogh paintings invoke an odd mixture of melancholy and serenity. Jackson Pollock paintings are kind of odd to look at, but they definitely engender some form of unique feeling.

There is a tension between the artist and the public here. The artist naturally wants to push their craft as far as possible: try to fictionally write or film the hardest to understand people, try to invoke the hardest to access feelings. The public only wants to feel feelings that feel pleasurable: the brutalist architecture definitely makes them feel something, but that feeling is negative, so they dislike it.

As it happens I've been rereading Paul Fussell's The Great War and Modern Memory just now (courtesy of my second grader developing a grisly interest in that war via the Nathan Hale's Hazardous Tales series; IYKYK). It's interesting on a bunch of levels and is just a hell of a book, but one of the angles that's really grabbing me that Fussell at least thus far hasn't really put forward is how closely the war coincides with the end of traditional poetry and its replacement with the stuff most of us ignore.

There are two obvious stories you can tell here (and I feel like they both have to be somewhat true). One is that the modern communication media that were about to displace poetry from mass culture were just hitting. Movies were in their infancy; the commercial gramophone was moving towards being a mass product; radio was soon to follow. Obviously this could steal the audience and leave the poets talking to themselves with no commercial incentive to produce stuff anyone else liked.

There's also the extent to which the war clearly shattered the entire cosmology of the participants, and left them grappling for new ways to express what they'd experienced. Dulce et Decorum Est is a fascinating blend of old and new, old allusions...but contradicted; old form...but with the rhyme scheme disrupted; unapologetically ugly subject matter and outspoken anger at the people who were using the old forms to write patriotic propaganda.

Fussell is particularly interested in a different work, In Parenthesis, which I now need to read; a mixed prose and poetic narrative of a soldier's experience from training to the Somme, which explicitly tries to reach back to Arthurian and mythological themes. Fussell's read is that Jones (the author) is trying to render the war comprehensible by fitting it into the old narrative tradition, but that the reality of life under artillery and machine gun defeat the effort; from searching around it seems that other people disagree about quite what Jones was trying.

In either case, you can see the outlines of a causal narrative; survivors of the war couldn't express that uniquely modern hell in the old forms, and since the art of the ensuing years was obviously going to be heavily concerned with processing the civilization's near self-immolation, things were going to move in a new direction.

(Side note: Fussell is sort of comically dismissive of the Americans, who both in his eyes lack the kind of strong national canon the Brits had and also didn't experience anything like the horrors the British did; he specifically roasts EE Cummings for seeming pleased with himself for being aware enough of Pilgrim's Progress to allude to it - incorrectly, Fussell feels.)

Which of these stories is right? Probably both, and you could probably loop them together into some broader "new media displaced the old popular media, new weapons created new horrors that called out for new modes of depiction" but it really does seem a hell of a coincidence when you put it like that.

> You move next to the painting to read the plaque, hoping to learn about the artist's inspiration. Instead you read: "Morning Light on the Valley by Sarah Williams (c. 1885). Scholars now believe many elements were lifted directly from an earlier painting by Agnes Dubois." The serene valley you admired a moment ago now feels… compromised? It's still pretty, but knowing it's largely borrowed deflates the sense of originality and genius.

---

Simply, my interpretation is that what you see is already shaped by what you know, remember, expect... The aesthetic experience is the total thing, context included, and that's what an artistic judgment has to work with, not some idealized version with the context stripped out.

Definitely food for thought. Perhaps it helps to compare art to history.

If you read a book about history and it explains some aspect of the Roman Empire, then you want it to be true. So, if you read it and enjoy it, and afterwards someone tells you that it was all made up, you feel betrayed.

Going further, some people are really interested in the Roman Empire, and perhaps they travel to Rome to see some monument that was build specifically for some victory of Trajan or so. And they see it and feel good. Now assume that they learn afterwards that the monument was actually erected in the 20th century and wasn't linked to Trajan at all. Then they are disappointed. Probably we would say righteously so. Truth is a important aspect of our expectation here.

But that is really close to how people feel when they visit art exhibitions of old pieces of arts. They don't care so much about the piece itself, they care about the historical context. So if it is made up, they have as much right to feel betrayed as someone who studies history.

Possibly, this is also true for new art: if I am interested in art that is 100 years old, in the context of its history, why shouldn't I be interested in art that came out yesterday, in the context of its own history, even though a lot of it is yet to happen?

All this is orthogonal to what Scott calls Beauty stripped of the placebo effect. But if you think that people neglect Best Art in Terms of Beauty, regardless of its context, then you should also promote the search for the Best History, regardless of its truth. Do you value the latter as highly as the former? If not, then why not?

Years ago, I tried to write science fiction stories. There was a local writing competition that also had some actual (i.e. mainstream) literary critics in the jury. Their decisions were often annoying. Like, in general, their taste was positively correlated with something being a good sci-fi story, but also once in a while they highly praised something that didn't make sense to anyone else.

From our position, they were just crazy. From their position, we (the authors disagreeing with their taste) simply didn't know what true art was.

So one year I decided to go full Sokal on them. Instead of trying to write the kind of story that I would like to read, I tried to optimize for their taste.

First, there was a guy who was among the winners practically every year. The competition was technically anonymous, but this one guy had a very specific style, recognizable immediately. From my perspective, he was just using the same pattern over and over again, and the critics were always impressed with the originality or something of his art. So this year I decided to write a story following exactly his template from the previous years.

Second, the critics always appreciated stories from new young authors, regardless of how technically badly written they were. So for my second entry that year, I tried to emulate a retarded teenager, and wrote a sci-fi poem containing the worst cliches I could think about. Added a sprinkle of patriotism, because that was another thing that some of the jury members valued highly.

Unfortunately, my first project failed, because not only the guy didn't contribute that year; he also wrote a letter to the jury apologizing for being too busy. So it was immediately clear that there was an impostor, and suddenly the template wasn't so artistic anymore. (One jury member admitted that before receiving that latter, he actually believed that it was that guy's story.)

Fortunately, the retarded poem made it to the finalist round, and got published in a book. We laughed about it a lot.

The long-term impact of my experiment was similar to Sokal's. The competition changed the rules, and the stories are no longer sent anonymously. That ended my participation.

Late to the party as I see you already posted a followup, but I wanted to add my two cents on restaurants. At a fundamental level, the system you describe where a restaurant critic has the food delivered in and eats it blindfolded is just missing major components of the experience. If how our taste buds reacted was truly all that mattered, people could just go about making the most delicious baby-food slurry and be content eating that. But you don't see products like Soylent transforming the eating experience. As a whole, society has not jumped on that bandwagon.

So in the first place, the visual presentation of food does matter. A perfectly browned, roasted chicken may be equally delicious to a pallid, beige chicken chili but one looks very appealing and one... does not. I've certainly seen many buffets or picnics where someone brought some casserole or side dish and absolutely no one takes it because it looks like cat vomit, which is a shame because it was probably delicious.

In the second place, your plan of restaurant critics having food delivered would - well, there's a vast difference between takeout and eating food that was made an hour ago or more and food that was made five minutes ago. You're going to get a severe downgrade in quality from that alone.

I thought your point about the diner food versus the critic rated steakhouse struck me as very funny because if you follow the great chefs, they are always talking about how the best steak sandwich they ever had was some hole in the wall in Bratislava or something. And they're inspired to recreate it in their restaurant but actually what they do is elevate it, deconstruct it, modernize it, and end up with something that seems to me totally opposed to both the substance and the spirit of this dish that they admired so much.

Now where I will slightly agree to your point is that on the whole, restaurant critics are reviewing Michelin starred restaurants, a breed known for their pretentiousness. When you eat at a Michelin starred restaurant, it's not just about sustenance or nutrition, it's not just about how the food tastes. Because you can get a perfectly good sandwich or whatever for 10 bucks. People who dine at those places are specifically going for the plating, the experience, the vibe, the artistry. When you're paying that much for one meal, they have got to pull out all the stops to deliver on very high expectations. They're not meant to be enjoyed by the common people who just care if something tastes good. A lot of us common folk just find those places pretentious and overpriced and don't understand the appeal. So it's a very good analogy to postmodern art in that there's a class of people who take it all very seriously and compare notes and pontificate about the symbolism or whatever, while a bunch of us look on in bewilderment.

From an evolutionary psychology perspective, art must serve some practical function in the human animal, assuming no divine creation.

Humans are intensely social, and many individual experiences simultaneously serve group-level functions: displaying status, defining norms, demarcating in-groups and out-groups, and aligning people toward common goals.

Religion is the clearest example. Individual experiences of rapture, guilt, and fear bind a society together; religious leaders direct the group; norm violations bring punishment or excommunication; dietary laws reinforce identity. It’s no coincidence that art is universally associated with religion: music, dance, architecture, sculpture, scripture, hymns, epics.

My argument: what we call “fine” or “high” art is effectively religious art for secular society. In our modern world, conventional religious functions are distributed across the state, academia, and cultural media—and are currently hotly contested.

While art has some inherent physical grounding (symmetry, mathematical relationships between musical intervals), taste is largely a social game. High-status individuals define it; others follow to signal belonging or avoid stigma. Taste ultimately orients a group toward its highest ideals—and away from what it condemns.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

(Yes, I used Claude to refine my initial draft and make it more readable. I am aware that I am signaling poor taste!)

Ask: I don't want to be surrounded by ugly buildings

I'm trying to figure out why, and I don't have a full understanding yet, but I think it goes like this: the upside of people taking out mortgages toward their own tastes in art, based on whatever combination of the 8 reasons you described above, in a decentralized manner, has a better net effect. You end up with places like the canals of Venice, CA, or the houseboats in Sausalito, or the flurry of modern homes in South Austin. These places have not only the sensory delight you're looking for, but a sophisticated pattern language that can only be achieved through this free economy of taste. Constraint consequentialists believe that you should try to do good things that improve the world, unless those break hard-and-fast rules (“deontological bars”).

For example, you shouldn’t assassinate democratically-elected leaders, even very bad ones. Why not? Since bad leaders set bad policy, and bad policy can kill many thousands of people, wouldn’t it be for the greater good? Because there’s always one gun-owner who thinks any given leader’s policies are bad, so without the rule, every leader would face constant assassination attempts, probably some of them would succeed, and the nation would either crumble or degenerate into a security state.

This explanation combines two sub-explanations. In the first, you are wrong about whether assassinating the leader would produce good consequences - you think it would, but actually it would produce instability, tyranny, etc. In the second, you’re right - maybe you’re a brilliant forecaster who can see that this particular assassination would end with an orderly succession by a superior ruler. But you know that there are far more people who think they are such brilliant forecasters than who actually are, and you either use the Outside View to suspect that you are also deceiving yourself, or at least realize that the only stable bright-line equilibrium is for everyone - true brilliant forecasters and wannabes alike - to refuse to act upon their apparent foreknowledge.

“Don’t kill people” is a gimme. What other deontological bars constrain our actions?

I’ve been thinking about this lately because of an internal debate in the AI safety movement. Some people want to work with the least irresponsible AI labs, helping them “win” the “race” and hopefully do a better job creating superintelligence than their competitors. Others want to pause or ban AI research - the exact details vary from plan to plan, but assume they’ve already thought of and written hundred-page papers addressing your obvious objections. Different people have different opinions about which strategy is more likely to help, and it’s possible to coexist and pursue both at once. But in fact, both sides are a little nervous that the other is breaking a deontological bar.

Some of the people working on pause-AI regulations think there might be a deontologic bar against supporting AI companies. These companies are racing each other to create a potentially world-ending technology. If one company’s product has a 90% chance of ending the world, and another’s has an 80% chance of taking over the world, giving your money/support/encouragement to the 80%-ers seems kind of like endorsing evil. I don’t know if it was encouraged by this question exactly, but someone held a Twitter poll about whether you would become a concentration camp guard if you predicted you could get away with being only 90% as brutal as your average coworker. Taking the job would have good consequences, but is there a deontological bar in the way?

Some of the people working with the companies think there might be a deontologic bar against certain types of mass activism. The sorts of arguments that do well on LessWrong.com won’t give us landslide wins in national elections. That’s going to require things like working with Steve Bannon, working with Bernie Sanders, working with NIMBYs who hate data centers because they’re a thing that might be built in someone’s backyard (or by non-union labor), training TikTok influencers create short-form videos about the dangers of AI, and holding protests where we chant vapid slogans outside AI company headquarters. There are better and worse ways to do all these things, but once you lay out the welcome mat, you have limited control over who shows up - and every time someone tries to create the Peaceful Nonviolent Pause AI Movement Based On Peaceful Nonviolence For Peaceful Nonviolent People, it spends an inordinate amount of resources keeping out violent crazies who want to tag along.

I would be better positioned to navigate this debate if I knew what deontological bars were or where they came from.

A common formulation is “act as if your maxim would become a general law”. This correctly rederives the bar against assassination, but fails even in some simple cases. For example, should the Ukraine abolish its military? If this became a general law, it would be great - it would end all war, and countries could spend their military budget on domestic priorities (or lower taxes). But doing this unilaterally would be disastrous. But most moral decisions are unilateral, so what remains of acting as if your maxim would become a general law?

Trying to resolve this particular loophole gets us something like “Don’t be the first person to defect from a generally functioning norm”. If no other country had a military or was planning to create one, then unilaterally building a military (and forcing everyone else to catch up) would genuinely be immoral. This also covers our assassination example: in a world where assassination is rare and effectively punished when it occurs, making the attempt yourself is defecting from the existing norm. In some alternative world where one party constantly assassinated the other party’s leaders, maybe the other party would have the right to join in rather than be constantly defected against?

(one problem with this formulation is that it’s hard to operationalize “generally functioning norm”. There will always be too-eager people desperate for some sign that the norm has become “non-functioning” so they can violate it at will. For example, there have been several assassination attempts recently on President Trump. I don’t think this makes the norm against assassination “non-functioning” or licenses retaliatory assassinations by Republicans - I don’t even think a successful Trump assassination would do this - but I’m sure some paranoid person somewhere would have that thought. I don’t know how to get around this and think it might require common sense.)

But this still doesn’t do it for me. Consider: should I use my blog to spread misinformation if I think it would have good consequences? Maybe if I found a very effective charity I wanted you to donate to, I could play up the benefits and minimizie its downsides to make it seem even more attractive? Nobody can claim with a straight face that there’s a generally-functioning norm against this kind of mild online misinformation. But it still seems like a good theory of deontological bars should say that I shouldn’t do this.

The best I can come up with is “Don’t do something which would be bad if universalized, unless the norm is non-functioning in such a way that you’d be playing cooperate while your enemy plays defect”. This lets Ukraine avoid disbanding its military - they would be “cooperating” with a “norm” so non-functioning that their enemies would surely “defect” by keeping their militaries intact. But it doesn’t let me spread misinformation with my blog: other bloggers might be spreading misinformation, but this isn’t a defection against me in particular, and it doesn’t doom me to automatically lose if I don’t follow suit.

(although again, this requires some interpretive work. Suppose I learn I’m getting 10% fewer subscriptions than I would if I spread more information, or that my political priorities are getting 10% fewer votes/donations, and this is directly because other bloggers who spread more misinformation are competing against me and winning. What now? I think I would have to conclude this isn’t enough losing to justify breaking the norm. But if not 10%, how do I know what number provides the justification? And do I actually believe that after reaching some number, it would switch from barred to permitted?)

How does this rule fare in the two cases I’m really interested in?

The norm of “don’t support an AI company” seems pretty thoroughly broken, now that there are many AI companies with tens of thousands of collective employees and hundreds of billions of dollars in investment. It also doesn’t seem like there’s some other group holding back on supporting the least-responsible AI companies who we’ll be defecting against if we support the most responsible AI companies. So I’m not sure what’s left of this one under the “don’t break unbroken norms” hypothesis - although I notice this would also justify taking the slightly-less-brutal concentration camp guard job.

(in order to turn down the concentration camp guard job, I think you have to strongly commit to acting as if everyone would follow your rule, even though you know it’s not true - but then how do we handle the military disarmament example?)

The political action campaign is slightly tougher. On the one hand, “don’t use mass politics to achieve your goals” is an impressively non-functioning norm! It’s hard to think of less well-functioning norms than this! On the other, if the Pause AI movement ended up exactly as scummy as the scummiest existing political movements (which tbc I don’t think they’re anywhere close to), then by definition they’re not breaking a norm - we posited some existing movements are already that scummy! - but it still seems bad. Maybe the relevant threshold is “don’t do worse than average”? Or “don’t do worse than your exact political enemies, who in this case are Leading The Future, Chris Lehane, and Marc Andreessen, so you’re probably fine?”

I think this is all defensible, and right now I don’t think either group is violating its particular deontological bar.

Of course, the Early Christian Strategy is to ignore all of this and do the right thing in every case, including unilateral military disarmament. But they can’t keep getting away with it, can they?

Well ... one version of "just do the right thing" is: "Morality" is just a set of quick & dirty heuristics. The hope is to find a set of simple rules that are easy to understand, that are consistent, that you can apply to all situations, and expect that it pretty much quickly guides you to behavior that you won't later regret. But all actual philosophical attempts at constructing such a code of ethics seem to wind up with inconsistencies, ambiguities, or at least an opposition philosopher can construct a disturbing hypothetical corner case where your moral code doesn't seem appealing after all.

But you can just abandon the attempt to find a simple uniform easily understood set of universal rules. Instead, just accept that each situation is unique, and it's easily possible that human preferences are not 100% consistent.

What you do instead is simple decision theory. At every decision point, look at the actions you have available, estimate the likely consequences of each action and the probability mass across the possible worlds that would result, and choose the action that maximizes your expected utility or general happiness with whatever world(s) would likely result. Stop searching for the heuristic summary of "doing the right thing", but instead just make a complete evaluation of each unique case from (your) first principles.

Maybe there's too much uncertainty to make a confident decision. Maybe you don't know what your preference is between the different sets of possible future worlds. In that case, don't worry about it! But when you clearly WOULD prefer one probability mass over another, then just choose that action in that moment.

And don't worry about whether your full set of decision choices over your lifetime, is easily described by a simple list of logically coherent rules.

Or perhaps you feel that you and your family are more important (for your own actions) than the welfare of strangers? Or perhaps you're after "pleasure for the greatest number of people" ... but then you fall into the Repugnant Conclusion?

So I was actually attempting to be serious about: Don't try to summarize the morality in a small paragraph. Don't even seek global consistency. Just evaluate each scenario in isolation, and do your own decision theory calculation for that specific scenario.

For the military disbanding, there's two more arguments why it's bad. One is that "no military at all" is an unstable equilibrium - the first country to get one will conquer the world - but we have a better alternative where countries can arm up as needed (but no further) which is both more stable and converges to peace.

The other is that when you universalize a principle, you universalize it more for people similar to you. It'll be very rare that your _only_ choices are, for example, to become a concentration camp guard or an SS trooper. (It does happen sometimes. This is not a personal moral position. It's a partly grounded belief about external reality, which is personally preferable to the more pessimistic alternative belief that would constrain you to the undesirable behavior.

"Do I really believe the world is so bad that my best choice is to become a murderer and forever distort my country's politics?" ... No, probably not. In short: it's unlikely that either of your examples would be ruled out by a deontological bar unless they're already impermissible on consequentialist grounds - but I'm unsure whether contemporary deontology is actually what you had in mind.

It's notable that the decision-theory-adjacent conception of deontology that you suggest, which is something like "deontology as a hypothetical coordination mechanism", isn't necessarily deontological. E.g. that reasoning is a major motivation for rule utilitarianism against act utilitarianism.

Contemporary deontology tends to be pretty heterogeneous (but then again, so does every philosophical tendency). Its proponents often use the term "non-consequentialism" to describe the tendency as it's easier to see what they're united against than anything they're united for.

So what *is* contemporary non-consequentialism if not a hypothetical coordination mechanism? Non-consequentialism tends to formulate particular moral devices which stick closely to our intuitions about particular cases - it's much more intuition-heavy and "bottom-up" than most consequentialisms. Examples include:

* A means principle - a benefit's ability to justify causing a harm is significantly reduced if the harm isn't an unlucky by-product of the benefit but part of the causal mechanism which achieves the benefit. This is why perhaps even a majority of contemporary deontologists would flip the lever in the original trolley problem, but very few would endorse killing and harvesting 1 person's organs to save 5.

* Adjustment for responsibility - a person's entitlements, e.g. to not suffer punishment, can be changed by their history of meritorious or blameworthy actions, even without any changes in expected future consequences.

* Excludable claims - we might want to exclude interests below a certain weight from consideration when much weightier interests are at stake - e.g. if a life is at stake, it doesn't matter that half the universe will get a paper cut; that simply shouldn't factor into our considerations.

Non-consequentialists do offer theoretical explanations which attempt to integrate particular devices into a wider philosophy, improving their theory's parsimony. Some pretty common theoretical moves are to suggest that the absence of that device cannot be be justified to a relevant constituency - the modern heir to the old social contract tradition - or to argue that it is needed to respect a special status held by moral patients.

Why do I think that non-consequentialists wouldn't have much to add for the two cases you consider? 4 reasons:

1. Non-consequentialists care a lot about causing and preventing harm. Most of the complaints about each side, even on non-consequentialism grounds, is whetjer each side prevents more harm than they threaten to cause - and that's the bigger, pre-existing controversy.

2. Most non-consequentialists think that side-constraints can be overridden when the stakes are high enough - and both sides believe that the stakes are *immense*.

3. In the case of people working on safety for AI companies, complicity is a real concern - but the attention of most non-consequentialists would be drawn to the difference between "is it permissible to intentionally harm someone if I deliberately harm them less than they would otherwise be harmed?", as in the case of the would-be concentration camp guard, and "is it permissible to attempt to prevent harm, at the expense of increasing the danger that that harm occurs earlier and by a different mechanism, while working to enrich a grossly unjust company?" The latter situation is troubling but easier to justify than the former.

4. That kind of mass politics is inevitable in a democracy, and non-consequentialists tend to be fond of democracies. Perhaps there's a stronger case if there's a major risk that the mass politics will overreach and cause significant injustice to non-culpable third parties? Perhaps a concern could be that it must involve deceiving people by deliberately misleading them about the reasons for you position? These both seem very hypothetical.

Re the Ukraine example, I think there’s a significant distinction between “having a military” and “using your military to invade other countries.” On the individual level, human beings have the capacity to commit all sorts of terrible immoral crimes, rape, murder, and so on. But original sin notwithstanding, we do make a moral distinction between having the capacity to do something terrible, and actually doing it. You can theoretically have a large standing army which just sits around waiting in case it’s needed, and while you might say that’s still morally wrong, I think it’s a different category of wrong from launching an invasion of your neighbour. We can also view violence in self-defence as a morally distinct category from unprovoked violence. That also distinguishes between the Ukrainian army case and concentration camp guard example: if it was possible to take the concentration camp guard job, draw your salary, and actually just sit at home, not turn up to work, and therefore not do anything morally wrong in the course of your employment, maybe that actually would be justifiable, particularly if it prevented the Nazis from hiring a more diligent concentration camp guard. But in practice of course the Nazis aren’t going to let you have that cushy sinecure, and even the 90% less cruel concentration camp guard is going to have to actually do terrible things in the course of their employment.

So maybe the multilateral principle works in cases of positive action, but not in cases about whether it’s acceptable to even have the capacity to perform a certain positive action.

This also seems relevant to the difference of the AI case, because part of the debate is about who is the actual moral agent whose decision matters here. If AI is just a powerful weapon, then you can make the same moral distinction between building it and using it. But the argument of the AI safety people is it’s more like a nuclear weapon that could just decide to launch itself. So having the AI companies or the government bound by laws and norms about what it can be used for, is about as useful for AI safety as my solemn vow that I will under no circumstances launch a nuclear first strike is a contribution to nuclear deterrence.

We might take some inspiration here from our understanding of biology. The general rule is that cells can do whatever they want unless and until they threaten the health of the organism that all of the cells depend upon for survival. If and when that happens, the immune system kicks (or at least it's supposed to) in and the transgressive cells are eliminated. Sometimes immune systems get confused, of course, which is what we call auto-immune disease, but the system generally works well enough.

Now suppose that instead of looking only at the cells and the organism they're apart of we zoomed out to coordination and competition among organisms or zoomed in to coordination and competition for energy and other resources among different biochemical pathways within the cells? I submit that we can find analogies to the same order we see established among cells — that is, that the basic rule is that each organism (zoomed out) or pathway (zoomed in) can do what it wants so long as it doesn't threaten the coherence of the structure one level up — that is, in the case of the organism, its colony of kin and in the case of the biochemical pathways, the cell.

Now we have a substrate we might use to establish an ethical principle: in most circumstances, it's best to maintain systems within some critical regime that maximizes adaptive capacity. In practice, this means don't let cells kill each other unless there's some cell that is threatening the health of the organism as a whole, then have the immune system take care of them. In the case of political action campaigns, it seems like the ethical target steers us toward making a decision based on whether or not the platform and or ideology of the campaign has the potential to undermine the entire economic and political order within which it operates. That was and is arguably true of a campaign built either explicitly or implicitly on an ideology like Carl Schmitt's, for example.
